question: What is the main goal of drug metabolism in the body?

options.A: To turn fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble compounds
options.B: To stop the kidneys from filtering chemicals
options.C: To keep drugs trapped in fat tissues
options.D: To make circulating medications more fatty

explanation: The body changes lipophilic substances into water-soluble forms so the kidneys can easily filter and remove them. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h1)

question: How does a prodrug differ from a standard active drug?

options.B: It leaves the body immediately through bile
options.C: It binds to plasma proteins without changing
options.D: It needs chemical conversion in the body to become active

explanation: Prodrugs are given in an inactive state and rely on metabolic reactions inside the body to start working. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which organ is the main site for drug metabolism?
explanation: The liver has the highest concentration of metabolic enzymes and receives a large blood supply from the digestive system. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h2)

question: Besides the liver, which other part of the body plays a big role in breaking down drugs before they enter general circulation?
explanation: The lining of the gut contains enzymes and transporters that break down drugs before they reach the main bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h2)

question: What is the main chemical result of a Phase I metabolic reaction?

options.A: Joining drug molecules together into chains
options.B: Attaching a large acid molecule directly
options.C: Causing drugs to clump inside the kidneys
options.D: Adding or exposing a polar chemical group

explanation: Phase I reactions unmask or add small polar groups, like hydroxyl groups, to change how the drug is structured. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h3)

question: Which process uses water to break chemical bonds during drug breakdown?
explanation: Hydrolytic enzymes use water molecules to split bonds inside drug structures. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h3)

question: Where are Cytochrome P450 enzymes mostly found inside liver cells?
explanation: CYP450 enzymes are concentrated heavily within the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why do genetic differences in CYP450 enzymes matter for patient care?

options.A: They destroy red blood cells immediately
options.B: They stop drugs from binding to blood proteins
options.C: They change how fast or slow a patient processes certain drugs
options.D: They stop the kidneys from making urine

explanation: Genetic variations mean some patients process drugs very slowly or very quickly, which affects drug safety and effectiveness. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of a Phase II metabolic pathway?

options.A: To turn inactive compounds back into prodrugs
options.B: To attach a large water-soluble molecule for easy removal
options.C: To store fat-soluble medications in body fat
options.D: To remove all polar groups from a drug

explanation: Conjugation adds bulky, water-soluble substances to make drug metabolites inactive and ready for elimination. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h5)

question: Which family of cellular enzymes helps with glucuronidation during Phase II?
explanation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases transfer glucuronic acid onto drug molecules during major conjugation pathways. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h5)

question: What happens when a patient takes an enzyme-inducing drug along with a regular medication?

options.B: The unchanged drug builds up and causes toxicity
options.C: Drug levels drop in the blood, which can cause the treatment to fail
options.D: The gut stops absorbing the drug entirely

explanation: Inducers speed up metabolism, clearing the target drug out of the body faster and lowering its active concentration. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h6)

question: What is it called when one drug blocks the metabolic enzyme activity of another drug?
explanation: Inhibition slows down enzyme function, leading to higher-than-normal drug levels in the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h6)

question: What term describes the amount of an unchanged drug that actually reaches the general bloodstream?
explanation: Bioavailability measures the percentage of an administered dose that successfully enters systemic circulation unchanged. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h7)

question: Why do oral medications often need a higher dose than drugs given through a vein?

options.A: The first-pass effect breaks down part of the drug before it can work
options.B: Stomach acid destroys every type of chemical
options.C: Oral drugs cannot cross any cell membranes
options.D: IV tubing absorbs all the active chemicals

explanation: Breakdown in the gut wall and liver reduces the amount of an oral drug that reaches the main bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a reason why drug processing varies among different populations?

options.C: Common local infections that affect liver function

explanation: Hospital architecture does not affect drug breakdown, whereas genetics, herbs, and illness do. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h8)

question: Why must nurses ask patients if they are taking traditional herbal remedies?

options.A: Local plants stop the liver from breaking down drugs completely
options.B: Herbal supplements always make oral drugs 100% effective
options.C: Herbs can speed up or slow down enzymes and change drug levels
options.D: Herbs replace the need for Phase II liver reactions

explanation: Many herbs interact with liver enzymes, which can lead to unexpected side effects or treatment failure when mixed with prescription drugs. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T3#GNS125_U5_T3_h8)
